2.text: Eeñeiˊvu, and carried a paper relating to the stopping of the war. Along

3.text: with that paper he took a large medal of silver.”

4.text: The paper in question, together with the medal, were actually preserved

5.text: in a Chukchee family on the Large Anui River. The owners put them in a

6.text: flat wooden box, and used this box in the ceremonial as one of the family

7.text: charms. I bought it from them. The paper proved to be a document dated

8.text: Feb. 8, 1789. It was directed to a “Chukchee Chaun Chief, Khamakhei,

9.text: who in the year 1788 expressed his desire to become a subject of her Majesty,

10.text: and to pay tribute, together with his kinsmen. For that promise he was

11.text: presented with a crimson coat, and with a parade dagger bearing the inscription

12.text: ‘Russian true subject.’ Thus all authorities would thereafter have to meet

13.text: him as a true subject and a slave of her Majesty.”

14.text: Khamakhei is the Chukchee name Qɪˊmɪqäi (“Little Worm”). Another

15.text: man of this name, whom Wrangel met on Cape Erri, may have been the

16.text: descendant of this first “true subject.” It may be seen from this document

17.text: that the Russian officials sought again to induce the Chukchee to become

18.text: subjects, and to pay tribute; but from this time on, it was done with great

19.text: caution, by means of persuasion and without any constraint. This policy has

20.text: not changed up to recent times, notwithstanding the fact that efforts were

21.text: made by a few officers to force the Chukchee into more real subjection.

22.text: The most active of all in this respect was Maydell.

23.text: Even the Russian Code contains special articles referring to “natives not

24.text: wholly subjugated.”¹ Of these articles, the 1254th says. “They are governed

25.text: and judged according to their own customs and usages, and are subject to

26.text: Russian law only in case of murder or pillage committed on Russian territory.”

27.text: I mentioned before that at the Anui fair only the inner space of the fort is

28.text: considered to be Russian territory. Outside the gate begins the free territory

30.text: Article 1256 says, “The Chukchee pay tribute in quantity and quality

31.text: according to their own free will.” This article, however, was excluded in the

32.text: next edition of the Code, in 1876.

33.text: Chukchee Tribute and “Chukchee Presents.” — In order to induce the

34.text: Chukchee to consent more readily to the payment of tribute, Banner obtained

35.text: from the Government a yearly assignment for the so-called “Chukchee presents.”

36.text: The sum was assigned from funds of his Imperial Majesty’s own Cabinet, in

37.text: accordance with the fact that tribute from the natives was turned likewise

38.text: into the same Cabinet. The sum varied greatly from year to year. Thus,

39.text: in the year 1791 it was 500 rubles; in the next year, only 85 rubles; a

40.text: century later, in 1861, and after that, it was 150 rubles. Maydell mentions

41.text: 143 rubles as the probable sum for the year 1869. With this money were

42.text: bought tobacco, kettles, and knives, which were then taken to the fair and
